[prose] Among the ecological traits examined, overwintering stage has the strongest effect on the species’ potential for multi-voltinism (Table 1). The proportion of multivoltine species gradually increases from species overwintering as eggs to species overwintering as adults, larvae and pupae (Fig. 4). The respective patterns within three major superfamilies largely coincide with the general pattern (Supplementary material Appendix 1 Fig. A1). In species overwintering as eggs, multivoltinism is remarkably rare: just 8.8% of such species are fully or partly multivoltine at least in some part of their European distribution range. The proportion of multivoltine species among egg overwinterers is low irrespective of host type and larval diet breadth (Supplementary material Appendix 1 Table A2, A3).

[prose] The proportion of multivoltine species is also low in species overwintering as adults: about a quarter of these species (25.5%) have a partly or fully multivoltine life cycle anywhere in Europe (Fig. 4). The proportion of multivoltine species in the subset of adult overwinterers passing the winter as fully formed adults within their pupal case (pupal imagoes) was similar to the proportion of multivoltine species among the rest of adult overwinterers (28.6% and 22.2%, respectively). Univoltine species among adult overwinterers do not exceed one-third in any host type and larval diet breadth category, except for in the species-poor category of monophagous adult overwinterers (Supplementary material Appendix 1 Table A2, A3).

[prose] There is also a tendency, although marginally non-significant, for the species’ potential for multivoltinism to vary with host type (Table 1). The gap in the proportions of multivoltine species is widest between species feeding on graminoid plants (grasses, sedges and rushes), and those feeding on forbs and low-growing prostrate shrubs (Fig. 5). In the latter, 62.1% of the species are multivoltine, whereas in species feeding on graminoid plants just 28.2% of the species are multivoltine. Twenty-one species feeding internally within grass stems are univoltine with just one exception. Species feeding on woody plants or both on woody and herbaceous plants fall between these two figures, with multivoltinism occurring in 52.9% and 41.5% species, respectively (Fig. 5). Species feeding exclusively on coniferous trees have a somewhat higher incidence of multivoltinism (61.1% of 18 species) than other species feeding on woody plants. In lichen-feeding species, 40% of the 20 species have a multivoltine life cycle.

[prose] Larval diet breadth shows no overall association with voltinism (Table 1). In all three categories, i.e. mono-, oligo- and polyphages, multivoltine species comprise slightly more than half of all species (56.2, 54.2 and 51.2%, respectively).

[prose] For each species considered, ecological data were retrieved from the most comprehensive (series of) monographs on European Macrolepidoptera available, with the series ‘Noctuidae Europeae’ (vol. 1–13, 1990–2011) and ‘The Geometrid moths of Europe’ (vol. 1–6, 2001–2019) providing data for the highest number of species (see ‘Data sources’, for a full list of data sources; also some unpublished and expert data were used). The voltinism (= number of generations per year) of a species, the primary response variable in the analyses, was ascertained separately for the whole European distribution range of each species, and for its populations inhabiting latitudes higher than 60° (mainly based on Finnish data from Silvonen et al. 2014). In the analyses, all species were classified either as univoltine species or multi-voltine species. A species was considered univoltine if it has one generation per year throughout its European distribution range. A few species with a biennial (= semivoltine) life-cycle, i.e. species requiring more than one year for development, were also included in this category. By contrast, a species having two or more generations per year anywhere in its European distribution was considered multivoltine. Similarly, a species having a partial second generation anywhere in its range (i.e. some part of the population having a single generation whereas some part being bivoltine) was considered to have a potential for multivoltinism, and was thus classified as a multivoltine species. Note that there are very few species among the lepidopterans studied that have a multivoltine life cycle throughout their whole distribution range. At least the northernmost populations of the studied species are nearly always univoltine (or, in some cases, biennial).

[prose] Almost half (47.1%; 344 species) of the total of 731 widely distributed moth and butterfly species examined have just one generation per year (univoltine life-cycle) throughout their European range (Supplementary material Appendix 1 Table A1). In northern populations (Finland, above 60°N), about two thirds of all species considered are univoltine, confirming the general latitudinal decrease in voltinism to the north (discussed in Zeuss et al. 2017).

[prose] The probability of being invariably univoltine across latitudes appears to be associated with species traits, with certain trait values strongly lowering the species’ potential for multivoltinism. The model with the highest support (Akaike weight = 0.61, altogether 16 models) contained species size (relative importance = 1), overwintering stage (RI = 1) and host type (RI = 0.74) as predictors of voltinism. No other model received comparable support (i.e. $\Delta \mathrm { A I C _ { c } } \mathrm { \leq } 2 )$ Altogether, the fixed traits in the best model (i.e. species size, overwintering stage, host type) explained 44% of the variation in voltinism. The cross-model relative importance of larval diet breadth was low (RI = 0.21), and this variable did not appear in the best model.

[prose] with species’ phenologies (Altermatt 2010b, Diamond et al. 2011, Végvári et al. 2015): overwintering stage, larval diet breadth, host type and body size. 1) Based on overwintering stage, species were grouped as egg, larval, pupal or adult overwinterers. Close to 30 species reported to overwinter as fully formed adults within their pupal case (known also as pupal imagoes) were classified as adult overwinterers. This was done so because, unlike other (‘true’) pupal overwinterers and similar to adult overwinterers, pupal imagoes do not require extra time for pupal development in spring. In the overwhelming majority of Lepidoptera, overwintering stage is fixed and species-specific. However, two species, Pararge aegeria and Erebia ligea, reported to overwinter in different stages, were left unclassified. 2) Five categories were distinguished on the basis of host type used in the larval stage. A species was classified as a forb-feeder, if it feeds exclusively or mostly on non-graminoid herbs (= forbs) or/and low-growing prostrate shrubs (such as Vaccinium, Thymus or Calluna). A few polyphagous species feeding both on forbs and grasses were also classified as forb-feeders. However, a species strictly specialized to feed on graminoid herbs (= Poaceae, Cyperaceae and Juncaceae) was classified as a grass-feeder. Species feeding exclusively or mostly on woody plants (excluding low-growing prostrate shrubs) were classified as tree-feeders. A separate category was established for species feeding both on trees and herbs. Lichen-feeders were assigned a separate category, but due to their small number they could not be included in the main analyses. 3) Three categories were distinguished to quantify larval diet breadth: monophagous (species feeding on plants of a single genus), oligophagous (species feeding on several host plant genera of a single family, or on a few genera of a few families) or polyphagous (species feeding on many host genera of different host families; see Holm et al. 2018, for an identical approach). 4) Average wingspan (maximum distance from one forewing tip to the other forewing tip), calculated as an average of mean male and female wingspans, was used as the measure of body size. For a few species with short-winged females, this measure was based on male data only.

[prose] Ecological correlates of the species’ potential for multivoltinism were evaluated using generalized linear mixed models with logit as the link function. Voltinism was used as a binary response variable (univoltine versus multivoltine) in the analyses. Larval diet breadth (mono- versus oligo- versus polyphagous), host plant type (woody plants, forbs, grasses, woody + herbaceous plants) and overwintering stage (egg, larva, pupa, adult) entered the full model as categorical explanatory variables, and body size as a continuous variable. Due to missing combinations of categorical variables in the data set, interactions could not be included in the model, but were subjected to detailed scrutiny using descriptive statistics. [prose] The increase in the number of generations per year (i.e. voltinism) is one of the most commonly reported phenological responses to climate warming in insects (Altermatt 2010a, Pöyry et al. 2011). Nevertheless, the results of this study suggest that a considerable proportion of insect species are likely to maintain univoltine phenology despite increasing temperatures. The examination of 731 European moth and butterfly species with a wide latitudinal distribution (15° as a minimum) showed that only slightly more than half (52.9%) of these species are multivoltine in at least some part of their range. The rest of species have a single generation throughout their distribution range despite a high latitudinal variation in temperature and season length. My results show that a substantial proportion of the among-species variation in voltinism can be explained by species traits.

[prose] Species not reaching 45° latitude in the south as well as those with clearly disjunct distribution ranges within Europe (which usually means that the southern populations are restricted to mountainous regions) were not considered (163 species in total). Additionally, I also excluded all migratory and occasionally occurring species (71 and 44 species, respectively). The final list of species (731 in total) included only species forming resident populations in Finland. The latitudinal range (15 latitudinal degrees, about 1650 km) considered corresponds to a 6.5–8°C difference in mean annual temperatures (Helsinki, Finland 60°10′N 24°56′E: +5.9°C; selected European cities close to 45°: +12.3°C to +13.8°C). This latitudinal difference in mean annual temperatures is roughly comparable to longterm projections of climate warming (IPCC 2018). The actual latitudinal distribution ranges (and thus temperatures and day lengths experienced by different populations) of most species substantially exceed this minimum range required for species inclusion. Given the wide range of season lenghts over the latitudinal range considered, a species with a single generation per year throughout its whole European range was assumed to be obligately univoltine and retain a single generation per year with ongoing climate warming.

[prose] Larval diet breadth has no discernible overall effect on the species’ potential for multivoltinism. The proportion of multivoltine species among mono-, oligo- and polyphagous species is strikingly similar (51–56%). No doubt, in some cases, feeding on a single host plant species (or particular organs, such as fruits and flowers) that is available for a short period, eliminates the opportunity for multiple generations (e.g. Parnassius mnemosyne on Corydalis spp.: Välimäki and Itämies 2005; Eupithecia immundata on fruits of Actaea spicata: Ehrlén et al. 2015; Anthocharis cardamines on flowers and growing siliquae of Brassicaceae: Posledovich et al. 2015). However, the majority of strictly-specialized species utilize host species with less-restricted seasonal availability. Another plausible but to my knowledge untested explanation for multivoltinism in monophagous species is that being adapted to feed on a single host plant has allowed them to speed up their development, and pass multiple generations despite a shorter period of host availability and/or seasonally decreasing nutritional quality of the host plant. It should also be noted that classifying species by larval diet breadth across a large geographic area is not as straightforward as for local scales. On the one hand, several species that could have been classified as mono- or oligophagous at the local scale (e.g. for Finnish populations), were actually classified as oligo- or polyphagous species because of their much broader diet at the European level. On the other hand, a long list of potentially acceptable hosts in polyphagous species does not preclude a considerable preference for particular host species (Põldmaa et al. 2016).

[prose] Akaike’s information criteria were used for model selection and multimodel inference. The models with $\Delta \mathrm { A I C } _ { \mathrm { C } } \leq$ 2 were considered to be close to the best model (Burnham and Anderson 2002). To infer the relative importance of predictor variables, model averaging was conducted across models with all possible combinations of variables. The relative importance of each variable was calculated by summing Akaike weights across all the models containing that particular variable. The larger the sum for a particular variable, the more important it was considered relative to other variables (Burnham and Anderson 2002).
